design_detail: Systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42023430416) of randomized controlled trials of sleep medicines with a next-morning driving test (on-road or simulator) after bedtime or middle-of-the-night dosing. 26 crossover RCTs were included and 22 entered the networks, all in healthy volunteers (only one trial also had people with insomnia). Outcomes: standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP, weaving) as a standardized mean difference after the first dose and at the end of repeated nightly dosing, and the rate of drivers impaired by more than 2.4 cm SDLP relative to placebo (the change produced by a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 g/L). Nodes are drug and dose; zopiclone serves as a positive control. Benzodiazepines in the networks: triazolam, temazepam, flunitrazepam, lormetazepam and flurazepam; the rest are Z-drugs, orexin antagonists, melatonin-receptor agonists, antidepressants and antihistamines.
can_establish: How much next-morning road-tracking (weaving) differs between sleep medicines and placebo, and between medicines, in healthy volunteers tested 8 to 18 hours after a bedtime dose in randomized crossover trials, after one night and after a few nights of use.
cannot_establish: Effects in people with insomnia or in long-term nightly use beyond about two weeks; crash risk on real roads; outcomes other than weaving; or a reliable ranking for the benzodiazepines, each of which rests on one small trial with wide intervals (CINeMA confidence low or very low for every comparison).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included trials recruited healthy volunteers, mostly in the Netherlands, France, Belgium, Japan and the US; one trial (Leufkens et al., 2014) also tested 16 people with insomnia.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: RCTs; people with a sleep-disorder diagnosis or healthy participants; next-morning on-road or simulated driving after bedtime or middle-of-the-night dosing; FDA-approved hypnotics or commonly used unapproved ones (melatonin, zopiclone, trazodone, mirtazapine, hydroxyzine, quetiapine); reporting lateral position. Excluded: conditions impairing wakefulness (narcolepsy, sleep apnoea, alcohol or sedative use disorder, brain injury), augmentation, tests shortly after dosing, non-randomized designs; crossover trials only if free of period and carry-over effects. No language or sample-size restriction (manuscript pp. 4-5).
sample.demographics: Mostly adults aged 20 to 65; three studies in people older than 65 (n = 243). Benzodiazepine trials: triazolam (Kay et al., 2016; 59 participants aged 25 to 55, 78% men, simulator, low risk of bias, sponsor Pfizer); temazepam (Leufkens and Vermeeren, 2009; 18 aged 55 to 75, on-road, high risk); flunitrazepam (Bocca et al., 2011; 16, mean age 60, simulator, some concerns); lormetazepam (Volkerts et al., 1992; 18 men aged 25 to 31, on-road, two nights, low risk); flurazepam (Vermeeren et al., 1998a; 24 women aged 22 to 45, on-road, three nights, low risk, sponsor Schering) (Table 1, manuscript pp. 9-16).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; one full text could not be retrieved (manuscript p. 7).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers rather than people with insomnia, mostly single doses, mostly from a small number of Dutch driving laboratories; several trials sponsored by the makers of the drugs tested. The authors note that people with insomnia may be less (or differently) affected (manuscript p. 24).

exposure.measurement: Drug and dose as randomized in each crossover trial; nodes defined by molecule and dose (manuscript p. 6).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only (Table 1): triazolam 0.5 mg; temazepam 20 mg; flunitrazepam 1 mg; lormetazepam 1 mg for two nights; flurazepam 30 mg for three nights (labelled 20 mg in the Fig. 2 legend); zopiclone 7.5 mg as positive control; oral, at bedtime, with driving 8.25 to 18 hours later (or 3 to 5 hours after middle-of-the-night dosing for some Z-drug arms). End-of-treatment analyses averaged 6.56 (SD 2.24) days of nightly use (manuscript p. 20).
exposure.polysubstance: Augmentation and combinations excluded; alcohol and other drugs controlled within the laboratory trials.

comparison.controls: Placebo within each crossover trial; zopiclone 7.5 mg as an active reference in many trials and in the networks.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover comparisons; network consistency assessed globally (Q) and locally (loop-specific) (manuscript p. 6).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; differences between trial populations (age, sex, setting, time of testing) are the main threat to transitivity.

outcomes.instruments: SDLP in cm from on-road highway tests or driving simulators; impairment rate defined as the proportion of drivers with an SDLP increase of more than 2.4 cm over placebo (manuscript p. 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The SDLP threshold corresponds to the weaving produced by a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 g/L in an earlier calibration study (Louwerens et al., 1987, as cited).
outcomes.operationalization: Driving impairment as more weaving than after placebo (standardized mean difference), or as an increase beyond the alcohol-equivalent threshold.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; many drug-dose nodes compared, with SUCRA rankings.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; most included trials were double-blind.

analysis.effect_sizes: First dose, SDLP against placebo (k = 21 studies, n = 2032; values from Fig. 2, an image read at its native resolution): triazolam 1.45 (95% CI 1.06 to 1.85); temazepam 0.03 (-0.56 to 0.62); flunitrazepam 0.32 (-0.28 to 0.92); lormetazepam 0.43 (-0.23 to 1.09); zopiclone 0.64 (0.51 to 0.77); zolpidem at bedtime 0.71 (0.10 to 1.31); zolpidem middle of the night, higher dose, 1.56 (1.09 to 2.03). Against zopiclone: temazepam -0.61 (-1.20 to -0.02), flunitrazepam -0.32 (-0.92 to 0.28), lormetazepam -0.21 (-0.89 to 0.46), triazolam 0.82 (0.40 to 1.24). End of repeated dosing, against placebo (k = 9, n = 806): flurazepam 1.65 (0.98 to 2.32), lormetazepam 0.44 (-0.23 to 1.10), zopiclone 0.42 (0.18 to 0.66); flurazepam against zopiclone 1.23 (0.52 to 1.94). Impairment-rate networks contained no benzodiazepine. Heterogeneity 0% and inconsistency not significant (p > .50) in all SDLP analyses; publication bias p = .0469 for zopiclone comparisons and p = .17 for placebo comparisons; CINeMA confidence low for five mixed comparisons and very low for all others (manuscript pp. 19-22).
analysis.covariates: Subgroup analyses by setting (on-road, simulated) and age over 65; sensitivity analyses excluding high risk-of-bias trials and unapproved drugs or doses (manuscript p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42023430416; protocol amendments listed in Appendix S7 (supplement not read) (manuscript p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Secondary driving measures (brake reaction time, speed, collisions) were deliberately not analysed (manuscript p. 24).
analysis.power: Not applicable; most comparisons rest on one small trial, and the authors name the few reports as the main limitation (manuscript p. 24).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In healthy volunteers, the morning after one bedtime dose, triazolam increased weaving well beyond placebo and beyond zopiclone; temazepam, flunitrazepam and lormetazepam did not differ significantly from placebo, but each estimate comes from one trial and its interval reaches as high as zopiclone's effect. After a few nights of use, flurazepam still produced large impairment, while lormetazepam's estimate was the same as after one night. Every comparison was rated low or very low in confidence.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions (manuscript pp. 2, 25) say most FDA-approved hypnotics at labelled doses paralleled placebo and that repeated administration reduced residual effects except for flurazepam, and the Discussion says one Z-drug formulation proved safe for driving; these readings treat non-significant results from single small trials as absence of effect, and the reduction with repeated use was not seen for the one benzodiazepine (lormetazepam) tested at both time points. Table 2 and the conclusions add prescribing advice (caution, discouraged off-label use).

timeline.event: Vermeeren's narrative review of residual effects of hypnotics, which summarizes many of the same Dutch on-road driving studies (cited in the Introduction)
Verster et al., pairwise meta-analysis of hypnotics and driving (cited; not in the library's references).
Roth et al., pairwise meta-analysis of hypnotics and driving (cited; not in the library's references).
This review: by the authors' account the first network meta-analysis of next-morning driving after hypnotics.

replication.where_it_stands: The only network meta-analysis on the question; its benzodiazepine estimates overlap with the primary studies summarized by Vermeeren (2004), so the two sources are not independent.

funding.funder: None (Role of the funding source, manuscript p. 25; abstract, manuscript p. 2).
funding.declared_conflicts: E.V. has received grants or fees from many companies, including Idorsia, Lundbeck, Merck, Sanofi-Aventis and Takeda, outside the submitted work; M.S. honoraria from Angelini, Lundbeck and Otsuka; M.F. rater for the Massachusetts General Hospital Clinical Trials Network and honoraria from ASCP, Angelini, Lundbeck, Bristol Meyer Squibb and Boehringer-Ingelheim; Ad.B. research support, lecture fees and advisory boards for several companies; others none (manuscript p. 26).
funding.affiliations_note: Several included trials were sponsored by manufacturers (for example Idorsia, Eisai, Merck, Pfizer, Schering, Wyeth-Ayerst; Table 1).

what_would_settle_it: Randomized crossover driving trials of the commonly used benzodiazepine sleeping pills in adults with insomnia, at usual doses after both one and several weeks of nightly use, with on-road SDLP and crash-relevant measures, powered to exclude an impairment equal to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.5 g/L.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can be judged only from Appendix S8, which was not read; if the list of excluded studies is missing or lacks reasons, confidence would fall to critically low. On the items that could be judged, one critical item (15, publication bias not discussed) is not met and two (2 and 4) are met in part, which gives low confidence. The review is registered, searched broadly, screened and extracted in duplicate and grades its own evidence as low or very low. For benzodiazepines its main limitation is not method but data: each benzodiazepine node rests on a single small trial, so non-significant results cannot be read as safety. Cite it for the direction and size of next-morning weaving after triazolam and repeated flurazepam, and for the imprecision of the other benzodiazepine estimates.

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group laboratory trial at the US Naval Health Research Center: 80 healthy young men (good sleepers, light caffeine consumers) randomized in equal numbers to eight groups that combined a bedtime capsule (placebo, triazolam at two doses or flurazepam at two doses) with an early-morning capsule (caffeine or placebo) on two consecutive treatment nights and days; caffeine was tested after placebo, after the higher triazolam dose and after the higher flurazepam dose. Next-day sleepiness (Multiple Sleep Latency Test, lapses on a tapping task, Stanford Sleepiness Scale, visual analogue scale), five performance tests and two mood scales were measured repeatedly over both days.
can_establish: Whether a morning dose of caffeine, compared with a morning placebo, changes objective and self-rated sleepiness, test performance and mood on the day after a bedtime benzodiazepine sleeping pill (or a bedtime placebo) in healthy young men under laboratory conditions, and how next-day sleepiness compares between the two benzodiazepines at two doses each.
cannot_establish: Whether caffeine restores driving or other real-world performance after a sleeping pill (no driving measure, and performance differences were not significant); effects in people with insomnia, women, older adults, heavy caffeine consumers or people taking sleeping pills for longer than two nights; or effects of other caffeine amounts or timings. With ten men per group, absence of a significant effect on performance or mood is not evidence of no effect.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers: healthy young male students of the San Diego Naval School of Health Sciences, studied in pairs; both members of a pair received the same treatment (p. 161).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Good sleepers selected from a health and sleep questionnaire and interview; non-smokers; no more than three cups of caffeinated drinks a day; urine and breath tests negative for drugs (p. 161).
sample.attrition: Three pairs were replaced: two because one member of the pair fell ill and one because the pair ate a much larger breakfast than the protocol allowed (p. 161); data from replaced pairs not reported. One man in the HTRZP group was excluded from the sleep analyses as an outlier on the visual analogue sleepiness score; six men had missing lapse data from technical problems (p. 162-163).
sample.selection_effects: Well-rested young men who sleep well and drink little caffeine, tested in a sleep laboratory with no caffeine allowed: the people for whom next-day impairment from sleeping pills matters most (people with insomnia, older adults, people who take them nightly) were not studied.

exposure.measurement: Capsules given by the investigators in the laboratory; double-blind (p. 161-162).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: bedtime capsule at 21:45 (lights out 22:00, woken at 05:00) of placebo, triazolam 0.25 or 0.50 mg, or flurazepam 15 or 30 mg; morning capsule at 05:15 of caffeine 250 mg (the authors' estimate: about two cups of coffee) or placebo; two treatment nights and days; oral (p. 160-162).
exposure.polysubstance: No caffeinated drinks allowed during the 2.5 laboratory days; meals standardized, with breakfast at 09:30 so that food would not affect the early-morning caffeine tests (p. 162). Non-smokers. Alcohol not mentioned beyond negative breath tests.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Caffeine-free in the laboratory from Monday afternoon; usual intake up to three cups a day, so the placebo-morning groups were briefly caffeine-abstinent (not discussed by the authors).

comparison.controls: For the caffeine question: the matching morning-placebo group after the same bedtime treatment (PC against PP, HTRZC against HTRZP, HFLZC against HFLZP). For the hypnotic question: the four drug groups without caffeine against PP.
comparison.matching: Randomization of 80 men to eight groups of ten. The authors report significant pretreatment differences on the MSLT, with the PP group showing shorter sleep latency; they state that analyses of difference scores and raw scores agreed, and present raw scores only (p. 162).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Habitual caffeine intake by group, chronotype and sleep before the laboratory nights not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same standardized laboratory conditions for all groups.

outcomes.instruments: MSLT (sleep latency to stage 2, scored blind by the first author) six times a day from 07:00; lapses (gaps of more than 3 s in a 10-min tapping task) at 06:00, 10:00 and 14:00; Stanford Sleepiness Scale and 100-mm visual analogue sleepiness scale before each MSLT; four-choice reaction time, digit symbol substitution, card sorting, short- and long-term memory and paired-associate learning at 07:30, 11:30, 15:30 and 19:30; Profile of Mood States and a nine-item visual analogue mood scale (p. 161-162).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory sleepiness and performance measures; pretreatment MSLT mean 10.7 min, similar to published values for young adults (p. 166).
outcomes.operationalization: Sleepiness as shorter sleep latency on the MSLT, more lapses and higher self-ratings; impairment as poorer performance scores.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Multivariate analysis of variance across related measures as a guard against type 1 error, Geisser-Greenhouse corrected repeated-measures tests, and pairwise comparisons (Hotelling T2) only after significant F values (p. 162). Many pairwise tests over days and trials.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind; MSLT scored blind by the first author.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or intervals reported. Group means over both days (Table 1, p. 163), MSLT sleep latency in minutes: PP 6.32 (SD 2.54), PC 10.73 (3.74), LTRZP 9.92 (4.46), HTRZP 7.61 (3.79), HTRZC 12.60 (5.12), LFLZP 5.92 (1.47), HFLZP 5.47 (3.06), HFLZC 9.62 (4.66). Editors' calculation: caffeine lengthened mean MSLT latency by 4.4 min after a placebo night (d about 1.4), by 5.0 min after the higher triazolam dose (d about 1.1) and by 4.2 min after the higher flurazepam dose (d about 1.0), using pooled SDs of the printed group values (how these SDs were computed is not stated). Lapses: PP 7.38, PC 1.16, HTRZP 7.23, HTRZC 3.06, HFLZP 6.32, HFLZC 2.98. MANOVA group effect on sleepiness F(7,66) = 4.25, P < 0.001; performance only a trend, F(7,65) = 1.98, P < 0.07; mood no group effect (pp. 163-165).
analysis.covariates: None; raw scores presented despite the pretreatment MSLT imbalance.
analysis.preregistration_detail: 1990 trial; no protocol or registration mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only short-term recall of the memory tasks is presented because long-term recall and recognition gave similar results (p. 162); means for each mood scale item are averaged to save space (p. 165).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; ten men per group.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Morning caffeine made young men less sleepy on the objective nap test for most of the day after a placebo night or after the higher doses of triazolam or flurazepam (about 4 to 5 minutes longer to fall asleep on average), with the effect fading by mid-afternoon. Performance and mood did not differ significantly between groups; the higher-dose flurazepam group without caffeine was the sleepiest on most measures, and the triazolam groups were not sleepier than the placebo-placebo group, which itself had the shortest baseline latencies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract (p. 160) says caffeine significantly antagonized hypnotic-induced drowsiness and that flurazepam at the higher dose made subjects sleepier than all other groups; the Results show the higher flurazepam group was the most sleepy descriptively, with its comparisons against the triazolam groups not significant (P = 0.056 at best), and no significant hypnotic-against-placebo difference is reported. The Discussion (p. 165) says caffeine reduced performance impairment in the two drug groups but that the improvement was not significant.

timeline.event: Roehrs et al.: caffeine given later in the day did not reverse the sleep-inducing effect of daytime triazolam, but higher caffeine doses reversed performance impairment (cited in the Introduction; not in the library's references).
This trial: by the authors' account the only study of morning caffeine after a bedtime hypnotic.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial in adults with insomnia who take a benzodiazepine sleeping pill, testing whether usual morning caffeine changes next-morning driving (on-road or validated simulator) and reaction time, with women, older adults and habitual caffeine intake represented and caffeine abstinence before testing avoided.

domains.note: Random assignment stated without method or concealment; treatment was given by pairs, so the unit of allocation may have been the pair; significant pretreatment MSLT differences, with the PP group sleepier at baseline.
Double-blind capsules in a controlled laboratory; three pairs replaced for non-study reasons or a protocol breach.
One HTRZP participant excluded from the sleep analyses as an outlier; six with missing lapse data; data of the replaced pairs not reported.
Objective MSLT scored blind; self-ratings by blinded participants.
No protocol; many outcomes, days, trials and pairwise contrasts, with only selected memory and mood summaries reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A blinded, controlled laboratory trial, but randomization details are missing, treatment was assigned to pairs while men were analysed as individuals, the placebo-placebo group was sleepier at baseline and only raw scores are shown, and several exclusions are not fully accounted for. The baseline imbalance would inflate the caffeine effect after a placebo night but not after the two hypnotics, where caffeine had a similar effect. The trial may be cited for caffeine reducing objective sleepiness the morning after a sleeping pill in healthy young men; it cannot be cited as showing that caffeine restores performance.

Editors' calculation: caffeine added 4.4, 5.0 and 4.2 minutes (d about 1.4, 1.1 and 1.0).

design_detail: Single-author narrative review (Maastricht University) of next-day (residual) effects of benzodiazepine and benzodiazepine-like sleeping pills. Part 1 summarizes epidemiological studies of traffic crashes, falls and hip fractures (case-control, case-crossover and cohort studies, Tables II to IV). Part 2 compares drugs and doses using three chosen sources: an expert survey from 1989 to 1990 (45 experts; a technical report, Table VI), a 1998 meta-analysis of 812 experimental studies of 248 medicines (Berghaus; Table VII) and eleven studies with a standardized on-road highway driving test calibrated against blood alcohol (Figures 1 to 3). Ends with the author's categorization of residual effects by drug, dose and time after a bedtime dose (Table VIII) and advice to prescribers.
can_establish: As summarized second-hand, which benzodiazepine sleeping pills and doses impaired next-morning on-road driving in the standardized test (and by how much compared with blood alcohol levels), how expert ratings and an older meta-analysis ranked them, and what case-control and cohort studies up to about 2002 reported on crashes, falls and hip fractures in people prescribed them.
cannot_establish: Pooled or appraised effect sizes (no systematic search, no pooling, no formal appraisal); whether the accident associations are causal (observational studies with confounding by indication, as the author notes); effects in people with insomnia who take the pills for months or years; or anything published after about 2003.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited epidemiology: for example a Saskatchewan cohort of 225 796 people prescribed a benzodiazepine and 97 862 controls (Neutel), a UK case-crossover study of 19 386 drivers in a first traffic accident (Barbone et al., 1998), and studies of adults over 65 (Hemmelgarn et al., 1997; Leveille et al., 1994; Ray et al., 1992) (Table II, p. 306). Driving-test studies were in healthy volunteers or women with insomnia who had used hypnotics before (p. 316).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated. The author chose to rely mainly on the expert survey, the Berghaus meta-analysis and the standardized driving test because studies differ too much to compare (p. 299).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The meta-analysis drew mostly on studies of 12 or fewer participants, usually healthy young men (p. 315).
sample.selection_effects: Driving-test evidence comes from one research tradition (Dutch on-road test laboratories, largely the author's group); experimental studies are mostly single doses in healthy volunteers; epidemiological studies can show risks only for commonly prescribed drugs (p. 314).

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: prescription records or interviews in the epidemiological studies; administered doses in the experimental studies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as summarized: bedtime doses of flunitrazepam 1 and 2 mg, flurazepam 15 and 30 mg, loprazolam 1 and 2 mg, lormetazepam 1 and 2 mg, nitrazepam 5 and 10 mg, temazepam 20 mg, triazolam 0.125, 0.25 and 0.5 mg, zaleplon 10 and 20 mg, zolpidem 10 and 20 mg and zopiclone 7.5 mg (p. 299); driving tests 10 to 11 hours after a bedtime dose and, in six studies, again 16 to 17 hours after; some after two nights or a week of nightly use (p. 316, p. 322).
exposure.polysubstance: Epidemiological studies: use of several drugs together is described as a consistent risk factor for falls and fractures (pp. 311, 313); alcohol use generally not separable in the prescription-record studies.

comparison.controls: Placebo in the experimental studies; non-exposed periods or people in the epidemiological studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The author notes that insomnia itself, the reason for prescribing and prescribers' choices (for example safer drugs for frailer patients) can confound the epidemiological comparisons (p. 314).

outcomes.instruments: Epidemiology: injurious crashes, police-reported accidents, falls and hip or femur fractures. Experiments: expert ratings of impairment (0 none to 3 severe) by time after dosing; percentage of performance measures significantly worse than placebo (Berghaus); standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP, weaving) in a one-hour, 100-km on-road highway drive (p. 316).
outcomes.validity_norms: The on-road test was calibrated in 24 social drinkers: blood alcohol concentrations of 0.5, 0.8 and 1.0 g/L raised SDLP by 2.4, 4.2 and 5.1 cm on average; test-retest reliability r = 0.7 to 0.9 (p. 316).
outcomes.operationalization: Residual impairment expressed as the alcohol level that would produce the same weaving.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the cited studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Second-hand figures: on-road driving 10 to 11 hours after a bedtime dose was impaired more than at a blood alcohol concentration of 1.0 g/L after flurazepam 30 mg and loprazolam 2 mg; at levels equivalent to 0.5 to 0.8 g/L after nitrazepam 10 mg, flunitrazepam 2 mg, zopiclone 7.5 mg, oxazepam 50 mg, lormetazepam 2 mg capsules and flurazepam 15 mg; not significantly after lormetazepam 1 mg capsules, temazepam 20 mg soft capsules or nitrazepam 5 mg (p. 316). Traffic crashes: odds ratios after a new hypnotic prescription 6.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 22.5) in weeks 1 to 2 and 3.9 (1.9 to 8.3) in weeks 1 to 4, falling to 1.4 in the second month (Neutel); 1.2 (0.8 to 1.7) for hypnotics and 2.2 (1.5 to 3.1) for anxiolytic benzodiazepines in a case-crossover study (Barbone et al.) (Table II, p. 306).
analysis.covariates: As in the cited studies; not summarized.
analysis.selective_reporting: Driving-test results are shown only for the studies with comparable procedures (Figures 1 to 3); others are described in text.
analysis.power: The author notes that most experimental studies were too small to detect minor or moderate impairment and most epidemiological studies too small for rarely prescribed drugs (pp. 314-315).

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized: several benzodiazepine sleeping pills, especially long-acting ones and higher doses, impaired next-morning driving in on-road tests by as much as or more than alcohol at common legal limits, while some lower doses of shorter-acting ones did not detectably impair it; use of sleeping pills was associated with more crashes, mostly early after starting, and with falls and hip fractures in older people, with inconsistent results across studies.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions (pp. 297-298, 323-324) present the summary table as a quick reference that lets clinicians choose drugs and doses unlikely to produce residual effects; this categorization mixes measured results with expert opinion from 1989 to 1990 and the author's judgment, and the categories 'unlikely' rest largely on non-significant results in small studies.

This narrative review.

replication.where_it_stands: Its driving-test summary is broadly consistent with the later network meta-analysis (flurazepam and triazolam impairing; temazepam and low-dose lormetazepam not detectably so), but the two share primary studies and are not independent.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a reported search and appraisal of on-road and simulator driving trials of each benzodiazepine sleeping pill, plus prescription-linked crash studies that separate sleeping pills from daytime anxiolytics and model time since starting, with results for people with insomnia who take the pills nightly for months.

design_detail: Scoping review with thematic narrative synthesis of 35 sources on harm-reduction approaches for benzodiazepine use (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit and novel benzodiazepines). Searches of PsycINFO, MEDLINE, Web of Science and Embase (14 February to 30 March 2024, rerun 7 July 2025; no date limits) with terms for harm reduction, overdose prevention, prescription misuse or diversion combined with benzodiazepine names; reference lists screened; titles and abstracts screened independently in duplicate by four reviewers after a 40-record calibration. Registered on the Open Science Framework as a systematic review and reframed as a scoping review because of the heterogeneity of designs; no risk-of-bias appraisal, no exclusion by quality and no meta-analysis. Sources grouped as direct interventions (drug checking, agonist treatment), policy (rescheduling, prescribing, toxicosurveillance) and population-specific approaches; Appendix 1 tabulates every source. Appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist: it maps without appraising, so it is not rated as a systematic review.
can_establish: Which harm-reduction approaches for benzodiazepine use had been described in the peer-reviewed literature indexed in four databases up to July 2025 (as far as the term harm reduction and the listed drug names capture them), in which populations, countries and settings, with what kinds of study, and where evaluations are missing.
cannot_establish: Whether any approach reduces harm or is safe (no included study was appraised, nothing was pooled, and most sources are pilot, cross-sectional, qualitative, uncontrolled pre–post or descriptive), or what people do before or during benzodiazepine use beyond the few practices reported in qualitative, forum and pilot studies; the map is incomplete for practices not labelled harm reduction and for grey and peer-led literature.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (scoping review). Sources: PsycINFO (EBSCO), MEDLINE (PubMed), Web of Science and Embase, first searched 14 February to 30 March 2024 (183, 345, 382 and 940 records) and rerun on 7 July 2025 with the same strategy (230, 444, 482 and 1195 records); reference lists of included papers. Full search strings for the rerun are printed in Appendix 1. Grey literature and the resources of harm-reduction and peer-led organisations were not searched (Methods › Search strategy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Limitations).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: sources that described or evaluated a harm-reduction strategy, intervention or policy relevant to benzodiazepine use, at individual or system level, with benzodiazepines a primary or substantial focus; criteria refined during the calibration round; no exclusion on quality. Excluded at full text: no harm-reduction strategy (39) or not relevant to benzodiazepines (14). Language limits not stated (Methods › Study selection criteria; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Included sources by country (Results text): Canada 8, United States 8, United Kingdom 4, Australia 4, Thailand 2, Switzerland 2, Sweden 1, Ireland 1, Wales 1 (no matching source in Table 1), multiple 2, global or online 3. Populations: drug samples at drug-checking services, adults who use drugs at harm-reduction services, female sex workers, residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, inpatients and outpatients with high-dose benzodiazepine dependence, opioid substitution treatment patients, emergency-department and festival patients, online forum posters, young people, women and gender-diverse people, poison-centre callers (Appendix 1, Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: Searching on the phrase harm reduction (or overdose prevention, prescription misuse, diversion) is likely to have missed approaches not labelled that way, and the many names of novel benzodiazepines made an exhaustive search hard (both acknowledged); including any source that used the term brought in abstinence-focused policies (acknowledged). Peer-led and organisational resources were not covered. Eleven of the 35 sources are drug-checking studies, about half of them evaluations of detection methods (5 or 6 of 11, editors' count from Table 1), which drives the conclusion that drug checking is the most prevalent approach. None of the five authors wrote any included source (editors' check of the reference list).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The approaches mapped: drug-checking technologies (paper-spray and other mass spectrometry, gas and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry, infrared and Raman spectroscopy, fentanyl and benzodiazepine test strips); prescribed benzodiazepines as agonist or safer-supply treatment; rescheduling of alprazolam and temazepam gel capsules; clinic prescribing policies; emergency-department and festival toxicosurveillance; peer check-in networks; poison-centre counselling; and practices described by people who use benzodiazepines in qualitative and forum studies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable. Some included sources give prescribed amounts or describe amount-related practices; the card does not reproduce them.
exposure.polysubstance: Central rather than incidental: most included samples and people used opioids (including fentanyl), stimulants or alcohol as well; novel benzodiazepines were most often found in samples expected to be opioids; the review does not separate benzodiazepine-specific harms or effects from those of other drugs.

comparison.controls: No comparison at review level. Few included sources had any comparison: a case-note review comparing opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines with those not or only briefly prescribed them (Bakker & Streel); a survey comparing young with older participants (Calvo et al.); an uncontrolled pre–post pilot (Park et al.); an observational comparison of behaviour after positive and negative test-strip results (Gelberg et al.); detection by one analytical method against another (drug-checking studies).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the included observational and pre–post sources do not support causal attribution, and the review does not assess confounding.

outcomes.instruments: As in the included sources: analytical detection rates; self-reported behaviour after drug checking; prescribing and dispensing counts; isolation completion and adverse events; treatment retention and mortality per 100 patient-years; emergency-department toxicology; qualitative themes; call counts.
outcomes.operationalization: Harm reduction is defined from principles (policies, programmes and practices that minimise health, social and legal harms without requiring abstinence; Introduction, 8th paragraph), but inclusion accepted any source using the term, including abstinence-focused prescribing policies, which the Discussion says may not match those principles (Discussion › Limitations in current prescribing practices; Limitations).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooling. Numbers are those of single included sources as the review reports them (see key findings).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered on the Open Science Framework as a systematic review (10.17605/OSF.IO/JG97Q) and reframed as a scoping review because of heterogeneous designs and evidence quality; the change is stated in the Methods and Limitations. The registration was not read. The review says it followed PRISMA guidelines and does not mention the reporting extension for scoping reviews.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable. How data were extracted (by whom, on what form, whether in duplicate) is not described; the change of design after seeing the evidence is reported openly.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A map of 35 heterogeneous sources (by Table 1: 17 quantitative, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews, 1 policy analysis). About half of the drug-checking sources (5 or 6 of 11 by Table 1, editors' count) test how well drug-checking methods, mostly portable or point-of-care instruments checked against laboratory analysis, detect benzodiazepines or other drugs in samples; behaviour after testing comes from one uncontrolled pilot with 66% follow-up and one observational study. Agonist-treatment evidence is a COVID-19 isolation-hotel cohort in which 6 of 77 residents received benzodiazepines, a policy case study that collected nothing from the people it served, a mixed-methods study of harm-reduction services in 34 European cities and two qualitative interview studies; under prescribing, one case-note review found post-treatment mortality rising steeply among people maintained on benzodiazepines. No included source evaluated, against a comparison, a practice that people use before or during benzodiazepine use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes drug checking as having consistent positive outcomes across studies and says benzodiazepine agonist prescribing during the COVID-19 pandemic has yielded positive outcomes; the main Conclusions call drug checking the most prevalent and pragmatic strategy. The Results say a positive test-strip result on benzodiazepines resulted in a 20-fold reduction in use (Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph), a causal verb for an observational association that Appendix 1 describes as a reduction in quantity used. The positive isolation-hotel outcomes are attributed to benzodiazepine prescribing although they describe the whole programme. The Recommendations say a safer supply of prescribed benzodiazepines may protect against harms of illicit use, citing sources that did not evaluate safer supply (a drug-checking study, two qualitative studies and a rapid review). The Limitations concede that no risk-of-bias assessment was made.

timeline.event: Searches run 14 February to 30 March 2024 under an Open Science Framework registration as a systematic review.
Search rerun 7 July 2025 (7 sources added); published as a scoping review in Harm Reduction Journal.

replication.where_it_stands: This is the only review of harm reduction for benzodiazepine use on the editors' reading list for this topic. It shows how thin the evaluated evidence is: practices people use before or during benzodiazepine use (not using alone, having someone check on them, staying at home, keeping naloxone at hand) appear only as reported behaviours, recommendations or forum content, and none was evaluated against a comparison.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Mental Health Drugs and Alcohol Service, Barwon Health; Academic Regional and Rural Addictions Network; School of Medicine, Deakin University (all Geelong, Victoria, Australia). Clinical addiction services; no author wrote an included source.

what_would_settle_it: Controlled evaluations (randomized where feasible, otherwise cohorts with adjustment for confounding) of specific approaches for people who use benzodiazepines outside treatment, such as peer check-in or not-using-alone services, drug checking with feedback, or prescribed supply, with overdose, emergency attendance and death as outcomes; and a systematic review with risk-of-bias appraisal of the trials and cohorts that exist.

domains.note: Four databases, printed search strings, a rerun, duplicate independent screening after calibration and stated criteria. But the search hinged on the phrase harm reduction, grey and peer-led sources were not searched, criteria were refined during screening, language limits are not stated, the text's flow numbers are not fully reconciled (Fig. 1 not viewable), and one included source is missing from the reference list.
No appraisal of any included source, by design; effects are reported from pilot, uncontrolled and observational studies without comment on their designs.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No included source is by the review's authors.

The abstract speaks of consistent positive outcomes; causal wording for an observational association; programme-wide outcomes attributed to benzodiazepine prescribing; recommendations (safer supply) supported by sources that did not test them.

domains.domain: Balance of benefits and harms reported for each approach
domains.note: Harms are reported in the Results (unintended effects of rescheduling; a steep rise in post-treatment mortality among opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines), but the abstract mentions only positive outcomes of agonist prescribing. Practices of people not in contact with services, and peer-led resources, are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a scoping review (METHODS §5.3), and this one maps without appraising, as its methods say. Its search and screening are well documented, but its summary statements go beyond the designs of the sources it maps, and its counts contain several errors (see reporting issues). It may be cited for what approaches have been described for benzodiazepines, in which populations, and for the absence of controlled evaluations; claims about whether an approach works must rest on the primary sources, read and appraised in their own right.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 2351 records identified, 1048 duplicates removed, 1303 screened, 88 full texts assessed, 53 excluded (39 without a harm-reduction strategy, 14 not relevant to benzodiazepines), 35 sources included.

The rerun added 249 new records, 17 full texts and 7 sources (Methods › Search strategy, 1st paragraph); on the editors' reading the first search contributed 1054 screened records, 71 full texts and 28 sources, but the text does not say so and Fig. 1 (the flow diagram, an image) was not viewable.

key_findings.finding: Sources were grouped as direct interventions (16: drug checking 11, agonist treatment 5), policy (9: rescheduling 3, prescribing 3, toxicosurveillance 3) and population-specific approaches (10: online drug forums 3, people who inject benzodiazepines 2, young people 2, women who use drugs 1, novel benzodiazepines 1, poison-centre callers 1).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1

key_findings.finding: By the designs listed in Table 1 (editors' count), the 35 sources are 17 quantitative (pilot, secondary-analysis, retrospective, cross-sectional and implementation studies), 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 policy analysis.
key_findings.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1, Study design column
key_findings.note: The Results text gives a different breakdown that adds to 28; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Drug-checking detection: a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples in which benzodiazepine test strips and/or infrared spectroscopy had failed to detect or quantify it; portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry identified 62% of samples containing carfentanil and 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam exceeded 3% by weight), against 9% for infrared spectroscopy (59 samples).
key_findings.locator: Results › Direct interventions › Drug checking, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Laxton et al.; Gozdzialski et al.)

key_findings.finding: Counterfeit and unexpected benzodiazepines: of 139 samples expected to be alprazolam (Xanax) at a Canadian service, 33 (23.7%) contained alprazolam by infrared analysis; 88 of 122 (72.1%) tested positive on benzodiazepine strips; of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 2 (10%) contained alprazolam alone, 4 (20%) alprazolam with other active ingredients and 14 (70%) other active ingredients only (antihistamines, amantadine, etizolam or flubromazolam, synthetic cannabinoids, opioids including fentanyl analogues). In Toronto, 15 of 555 samples were expected to be benzodiazepines but benzodiazepine-type drugs were found in 116 (etizolam 95, flualprazolam 46); in a Canadian community drug-checking programme (159 samples, October 2018 to January 2020), 6.5% of the samples thought to contain opioids held unexpected novel benzodiazepines.
key_findings.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Tobias et al.; Scarfone et al.; Laing); Results › Drug checking, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine-type drugs were present in 41% (24) of the samples linked to a negative effect (adverse health event, extreme sedation or overdose) during a Toronto drug-checking pilot.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug checking, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Scarfone et al.)
key_findings.note: Presence in samples linked to a negative effect, not cause of the effect.

key_findings.finding: Behaviour after test-strip results: in a Baltimore pilot with 103 female sex workers who use drugs (68, 66%, completed the one-month follow-up), 84% used at least one strip, 86% had a fentanyl-positive result and 69% reported a harm-reduction behaviour afterwards (for example asking someone to check on them); without a control group, reported injection frequency fell from 40% to 25%, benzodiazepine use from 22% to 7% and using alone from 96% to 68%. In a US observational study of 541 adults over 28 days, a positive result was associated with having naloxone nearby, taking turns and using less; Table 1 reports a positive result associated with a four-fold reduction in quantity used overall, largest when benzodiazepines were tested (20-fold, against 10-fold for stimulants and 2-fold for opioids).
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug checking, 3rd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Park et al.; Gelberg et al.)
key_findings.note: Completers only in the pilot; association only in the observational study, though the Results text says the positive result resulted in the reduction.

key_findings.finding: Agonist (prescribed) benzodiazepine treatment: in COVID-19 isolation hotels in Canada, 6 of 77 residents (8%) received prescribed benzodiazepines within a safe-supply and managed-alcohol programme that reported low adverse events, no overdoses and high completion of isolation for the programme as a whole; in Dublin more than 70 people experiencing homelessness started benzodiazepine maintenance, with staff-reported improvements in health and adherence and no feedback collected from the people treated (policy analysis).
key_findings.locator: Results › Direct interventions › Agonist treatment, 1st paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Brothers et al.; O'Carroll et al.); References, reference 55
key_findings.note: The isolation-hotel evaluation (Brothers et al., reference 55) is cited from a 2022 medRxiv preprint, so the outcome for the 6 residents prescribed benzodiazepines rests on a report the review cites as a preprint; the programme-wide outcomes are not specific to them (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: In two Swiss qualitative interview studies of 41 people with high-dose benzodiazepine dependence, participants preferred prescribed to illicit benzodiazepines (less crime, lower cost, less risk of contaminated pills); some reported their prescriber stopped treatment when non-prescribed use was discovered; people with repeated withdrawal attempts and hospitalisations preferred discontinuation to maintenance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Agonist treatment, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Liebrenz et al., two studies)

key_findings.finding: In an inner-London general-practice case-note review of 278 opioid substitution patients, the 127 maintained on benzodiazepines stayed in treatment longer (72 months) than those not prescribed them (34) or briefly prescribed them (51); in-treatment mortality was 1.31 per 100 patient-years with maintenance against 1.79 without; post-treatment mortality in the maintained group was reported as rising by 450% (to 5.90 per 100 years), against 191% and 125% in the other groups. Table 1 adds that patients with occasional benzodiazepine prescriptions had the lowest in-treatment mortality (no figure given), so the 1.31 against 1.79 comparison is with patients not prescribed benzodiazepines only.
key_findings.locator: Results › Policy › Prescribing, 2nd paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Bakker and Streel)
key_findings.note: The review does not say how deaths were ascertained (case notes of one practice). 5.90 is 4.5 times 1.31, an increase of about 350% (editors' calculation); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Rescheduling: a 2021 review found five evaluations of Australia's 2014 move of alprazolam from Schedule 4 to Schedule 8; four reported large declines in alprazolam use, with declines in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls, and further restrictions in 2017 had no substantial effect. The Discussion adds that alprazolam-related deaths fell from 57 (2012) to 23 (2015) while overall benzodiazepine overdose deaths rose from 160 (2009) to 238 (2015).
key_findings.locator: Results › Policy › Rescheduling, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Latent impacts of rescheduling
key_findings.note: The death counts come from a letter (Lloyd et al., 2017, reference 82), and the declines in overdose deaths from the 2021 review's summary; for neither does the review say how deaths were identified, coded or attributed, or by whom (alprazolam-related and benzodiazepine overdose are its words), and the two series start in different years. Reference 82 is a two-page response letter (Int J Drug Policy 2017;39:138–9).

key_findings.finding: Temazepam gel capsules: after UK rescheduling, 100 people with long-term polydrug use reported less injection of gel capsules but continued injection of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime and substitution with flunitrazepam (qualitative). In a Melbourne ethnography, one participant described using temazepam at home at the end of the day to avoid losing money or drugs, or arrest, while sedated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Policy › Rescheduling, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Fountain et al.; Dwyer)

key_findings.finding: A 'no benzodiazepine' formulary policy in six Kentucky outpatient mental health clinics (2016) was followed by an 89% fall in benzodiazepine prescriptions over two years without a fall in caseloads; the Discussion says that approaches like this one, which enforced cessation as a non-negotiable outcome, may differ from core harm-reduction principles.
key_findings.locator: Results › Policy › Prescribing, 1st paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Agrawal et al.); Discussion › Limitations in current prescribing practices, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Kentucky is named only in Table 1; the Results text says six outpatient mental health clinics in the United States.

key_findings.finding: Toxicosurveillance in Victoria, Australia: of 1112 emergency-department presentations with drug toxicity (2020–2022), 183 (16.5%) involved benzodiazepine-type novel substances (median age 24), 12 different ones, clonazolam and etizolam most often, nearly half with more than one, often with methamphetamine and with prescription benzodiazepines not disclosed by the patient. At music festivals, 24 severely unwell patrons (of 228 drug-toxicity presentations) reported a median of two drugs but toxicology found a median of four, and nearly half had novel psychoactive substances present though none reported taking them intentionally.
key_findings.locator: Results › Policy › Toxicosurveillance, 1st paragraph; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Syrjanen et al., references 66 and 67)

key_findings.finding: Practices described by people who use benzodiazepines: on a Swedish forum about flubromazolam (N=122 in Table 1), posters shared practices such as limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, qualitative) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in Bangkok, a survey of 252 people who inject drugs led its authors to call for education against injecting alone, among other measures.
key_findings.locator: Appendix 1, Table 1 (Andersson and Kjellgren; Speed et al.; Kerr et al.); Results › Population-specific approaches › Women who use drugs; People who inject benzodiazepines
key_findings.note: Reported practices and recommendations; none was evaluated against a comparison. Forum content on amounts is not reproduced.

key_findings.finding: Young people (18–30) at New York City harm-reduction programmes (257 of 2251 participants) were more likely than older participants to report a recent overdose and less likely to know about naloxone; past-year overdose among them went with psychological distress, unstable housing or homelessness, and use of detoxification.
key_findings.locator: Results › Population-specific approaches › Young people; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Calvo et al.)

key_findings.finding: Social workers answering a US poison centre's tablet-identification line handled 17,616 calls in 20 months and gave overdose-prevention or safety information to 6635 callers (37.7%); the service was judged feasible, without outcome evaluation.
key_findings.locator: Results › Population-specific approaches › Poison centre callers; Appendix 1, Table 1 (Doyon et al.)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that drug checking is the most prevalent and pragmatic approach, that prescribing and policy interventions had mixed effects, and that harm-reduction interventions are notably absent for people not seeking abstinence or formal treatment; they acknowledge that the term-based search may have missed studies, that no risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was done, and that peer-led resources were not covered.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Limitations

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says the sources were 20 quantitative, 1 qualitative, 4 reviews, 2 mixed-methods and 1 policy analysis, which adds to 28, not 35; Table 1 lists 17 quantitative, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 policy analysis (editors' count), and the Results themselves describe at least four qualitative studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The design profile must be taken from Table 1; the text's figure of one qualitative study is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The countries listed in the Results text add to 36, not 35, and include Wales (1), which matches no source in Table 1 (the four United Kingdom sources are counted separately).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite countries from Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the first search's record counts (183, 345, 382, 940; 1850 in all, editors' sum), while the Results report 2351 records identified, which equals the July 2025 rerun counts. The rerun paragraph (duplicates removed in two stages, 218 and 127, leaving 249 new records, 17 full texts, 7 inclusions) is not reconciled with 1303 screened and 88 full texts in the text, and Fig. 1, the flow diagram, is an image that could not be viewed here. The rerun's own counts (230 + 482 + 444 + 1195 = 2351) less the two duplicate stages (218 + 127) leave 2006, not 249, so the 249 can only be records not already found by the first search, which the text does not say (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The numbers are consistent if 1303 screened = 1054 from the first search + 249 new (and 88 = 71 + 17; 35 = 28 + 7), but the paper does not say so; cite only 35 included sources and 88 full texts.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation errors: the included European COVID-19 study (Rigoni et al., on harm-reduction services in 34 European cities) is cited as reference 32, but reference 32 is a different Rigoni paper (Jakarta, 2019), and the included study is not in the reference list. The prescribing paragraph cites references 62–64, but 63 is a 1997 study of amphetamine prescribing, while the third source described is reference 65; Table 1 labels Guina et al. as 65, which is 64 in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the 35 sources cannot be traced from the reference list; claims drawing on the agonist-treatment or prescribing sections should be checked against the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say a positive fentanyl test-strip result on benzodiazepines resulted in a 20-fold reduction in use; Table 1 describes an observational association with the quantity used. The Results also attribute the isolation-hotel programme's low adverse events, absence of overdoses and completed isolation to benzodiazepine prescribing, while Table 1 shows these outcomes for all 77 residents, of whom 6 received benzodiazepines.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither source shows that the approach caused the outcome; the agonist-treatment evidence for benzodiazepines in that cohort rests on 6 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Post-treatment mortality among opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines is reported as rising by 450% to 5.90 per 100 years from an in-treatment rate of 1.31, but 5.90 is 4.5 times 1.31, an increase of about 350% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentage appears to be a ratio stated as an increase, by the review or by the primary paper; check the primary paper before citing either figure. How the deaths were ascertained is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The alprazolam death comparison (related deaths down 60% from 2012 to 2015; overall benzodiazepine overdose deaths up 49% from 2009 to 2015) is described as covering a similar period, but the two series start in different years, and neither the definitions of the deaths nor who attributed them are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast cannot show substitution or displacement of deaths; the source letter (Lloyd et al., 2017) would be needed to know how deaths were counted.

reporting_issues.issue: Background figures in the Introduction: the United Kingdom figure for deaths involving benzodiazepines (9.7 per million in 1997 to 17.8 in 2022) is cited to an Office for National Statistics bulletin on deaths related to drug poisoning in England and Wales; the United States rise from 1145 deaths (1999) to 10,964 (2022) is called eightfold, though it is 9.6 times; and 902 of 1337 border detections is given as 64%, though it is 67.5% (editors' calculations). None of the death figures says how deaths were defined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Background only; none of these figures should be cited from this review.

design_detail: Nested case-control study in the Quebec public health-insurance claims database (RAMQ), 2000–2009: 1,796 community-dwelling people aged over 66 with a first claims diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (ICD-9 331.0) and at least 6 years of prior follow-up, each matched to 4 controls (7,184) on sex, age group and length of follow-up by incidence density sampling. Exposure: benzodiazepine dispensing claims in the window 5 to 10 years before the index date (treatment started in the last 5 years ignored), as ever use, cumulative prescribed daily doses (1–90, 91–180, above 180) and half-life (under 20 h, 20 h or more). Conditional logistic regression with two adjustment sets; sensitivity analysis with a 6-year lag.
can_establish: Whether older Quebec residents later given a claims diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years earlier more often than matched controls, and whether the difference grew with cumulative amount and half-life.
cannot_establish: That benzodiazepines cause Alzheimer's disease: the reasons for prescribing (anxiety, insomnia, depression), symptoms that may precede diagnosis by more than the 5-year lag, education, socioeconomic status, smoking and alcohol were unmeasured or poorly measured; nor absolute risks or numbers of excess cases (case-control design), nor effects in younger adults.

sample.recruitment: Registry: random samples of the RAMQ drug-plan population aged over 66 living in the community, 38,741 with a dementia diagnosis or treatment (source of cases) and 86,259 without (source of controls) (p. 2). About 98% of older Quebec residents are covered by the plan (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cases: first recorded diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (ICD-9 331.0) in 2000–2009, no earlier record of another type of dementia, no anti-dementia treatment before the index date, and at least 6 years of follow-up before it (p. 2). Of the 38,741 sampled people with dementia-related claims, 31,769 were excluded for non-Alzheimer dementia or anti-dementia treatment before diagnosis and 5,176 for under 6 years of follow-up, leaving 1,796 (Figure, p. 10). Controls: 4 per case by incidence density sampling, matched on sex, age group (70–74, 75–79, 80–84, 85 or over) and follow-up (6 to 10 years) (p. 2).
sample.demographics: 67.0% women; aged 70–74 13.3%, 75–79 26.0%, 80–84 31.5%, 85 or over 29.3%; identical in cases and controls by matching (Table 2, p. 8). Education, income, smoking and alcohol are not recorded in the database (p. 4).
sample.selection_effects: Cases are a narrow subset of people with dementia-related claims (1,796 of 38,741, 4.6%; editors' calculation), selected for a first Alzheimer code without earlier anti-dementia treatment; the two main exclusion reasons are counted together, so their separate sizes are unknown. Requiring 6 years of prior follow-up excludes people who joined the plan later. Controls were drawn from a separate random sample of people without dementia-related claims.

exposure.measurement: Pharmacy dispensing claims for the 13 benzodiazepines reimbursed by RAMQ (Table 1, p. 7), counted only in the window from 5 to 10 years before the index date; treatment started less than 5 years before was not considered (p. 2). Cumulative amount converted to prescribed daily doses (PDDs) by dividing by each product's average daily dose in the source cohort, so that 1 PDD is about one day of average use (p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Ever use = at least one claim in the window; cumulative 1–90 PDDs (up to about 3 months), 91–180 (3 to 6 months), above 180 (over 6 months); half-life under 20 h or 20 h and longer, the longer retained for people who used several drugs (p. 2). Because follow-up was 6 to 10 years, the window lasted 1 to 5 years depending on follow-up length (matched). Among people with any use, treatment was still active at the index date in 64.8% of cases and 60.6% of controls (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Z-drug hypnotics and other psychotropic medicines (antidepressants, antipsychotics) are neither mentioned nor adjusted for. Smoking and alcohol are not recorded in the database (p. 4).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. The reference group was people with no claim in the 5-to-10-year window (p. 2); as defined, it would also contain anyone whose benzodiazepine use began only in the last 5 years before the index date (editors' reading; the paper gives no count).

comparison.controls: 7,184 people without dementia diagnoses or treatment, drawn from the same insured population at each case's index date (pp. 2–3).
comparison.matching: Sex, age group and duration of follow-up, 4 controls per case (Table 2, p. 8).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Education, socioeconomic status, smoking and alcohol are unavailable (p. 4). Anxiety, depression and insomnia are known only as claims diagnoses in the exposure window, recorded in 21.4% vs 15.1%, 2.9% vs 2.4% and 4.0% vs 3.2% of cases and controls, against benzodiazepine use in 49.8% vs 40.0% (Table 2, p. 8); no cognitive or functional measures.

outcomes.instruments: Claims diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (ICD-9 331.0) recorded by a physician (general practitioner, neurologist, internist or geriatrician) (pp. 2–3). The authors note that cholinesterase-inhibitor reimbursement requires a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 10 to 26 and, for continuation after 6 months, evidence of benefit, and that these criteria were met in 72% of cases (p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation of the claims diagnosis against research diagnostic criteria is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Outcome = first recorded Alzheimer's diagnosis; index date = date of that record, and the same date for the matched controls (p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome, with ever use, three cumulative-dose categories and two half-life categories, each in two adjusted models, plus a lagged sensitivity analysis and a split by treatment status at diagnosis.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (routine clinical diagnoses); diagnosing physicians would usually have known patients' medications.

analysis.effect_sizes: Conditional logistic regression odds ratios with 95% CI (Table 3, p. 9); univariable, model 1, model 2. Ever use: 1.52 (1.37 to 1.69); 1.51 (1.36 to 1.69); 1.43 (1.28 to 1.60). 1–90 PDDs: 1.08 (0.92 to 1.27); 1.09 (0.92 to 1.28); 1.05 (0.89 to 1.24). 91–180 PDDs: 1.33 (1.01 to 1.75); 1.32 (1.01 to 1.74); 1.28 (0.97 to 1.69). Above 180 PDDs: 1.85 (1.63 to 2.09); 1.84 (1.62 to 2.08); 1.74 (1.53 to 1.98). Half-life under 20 h: 1.43 (1.27 to 1.61); 1.43 (1.27 to 1.61); 1.37 (1.21 to 1.55). 20 h or more: 1.72 (1.48 to 1.99); 1.70 (1.46 to 1.98); 1.59 (1.36 to 1.85). Six-year-lag sensitivity analysis: ever use 1.50 (1.35 to 1.68); up to 3 months 1.11 (0.94 to 1.30); 3 to 6 months 1.56 (1.21 to 2.01); over 6 months 1.79 (1.58 to 2.04) (p. 3). No absolute risks (case-control design).
analysis.covariates: Model 1: high blood pressure, myocardial infarction, stroke, platelet inhibitors or oral anticoagulants, diabetes, hypercholesterolaemia and a comorbidity indicator built from Charlson index conditions, all measured in the exposure window (p. 2; Table 3 footnotes). Model 2 adds anxiety, depression and insomnia diagnoses, entered because they did not interact with exposure (P = 0.48, 0.75, 0.99) (pp. 2–3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Ethics approval by the research ethics committee of the University of Montreal Hospital Research Centre (CRCHUM); no registration or published protocol is mentioned (p. 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: All exposure categories and both models are tabulated. The sensitivity analysis is given in the text only, without counts, with adjusted odds ratios apparently from model 1 (further adjustment for anxiety, depression and insomnia is said only not to have changed the conclusions); the split by treatment status at diagnosis is given only in the Discussion, without counts and without saying which model was used (p. 4). The abstract reports model 1 for the dose categories.
analysis.power: Not reported. 1,796 cases give precise estimates for ever use; the 91–180 PDD category contains 70 cases (Table 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Older Quebec residents with a first claims diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease had filled benzodiazepine prescriptions 5 to 10 years earlier more often than matched controls (49.8% vs 40.0%; adjusted odds ratio 1.43 to 1.51). There was no association for up to about 3 months' cumulative supply (1.09, 0.92 to 1.28); above 6 months' supply the odds ratio was 1.84 (1.62 to 2.08), with 32.9% of cases vs 21.8% of controls in that category, and it was higher for long-acting (1.70) than short-acting drugs (1.43). Adding claims-recorded anxiety, depression and insomnia changed little, but those diagnoses were recorded for only a small fraction of the people filling prescriptions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the stronger association with long-term exposure “reinforces the suspicion of a possible direct association” (p. 1), while allowing that use might be an early marker, and calls unwarranted long-term use a public-health concern. The implications section goes further, saying that a risk increased by 43–51% would generate a huge number of excess cases (p. 4): this treats odds ratios from an observational comparison as a causal risk and gives no absolute figures. The box on what the study adds states that there is a dose-effect relation (p. 5), while the same box and the limitations (p. 4) concede the link may not be causal. The 5-year lag may not exclude prodromal anxiety or sleep problems; education, socioeconomic status, smoking and alcohol were not measured; and adjustment for the reasons for prescribing rests on diagnoses missing for most people who filled prescriptions. A headline that benzodiazepines raise the risk of Alzheimer's disease by about 50% would overstate this paper: it shows an association in claims data, strongest with more than 6 months' supply, not an effect, and no absolute risk.

timeline.event: Fastbom et al. reported a paradoxical protective association, which this paper attributes partly to past use being counted in the reference group (p. 3).
Lagnaoui et al., nested case-control study, cited as congruent, though the authors say a protopathic bias could not be ruled out in it because of insufficient follow-up (p. 3).

Gallacher et al., Caerphilly Prospective Study, cited as congruent, though the authors say a protopathic bias could not be ruled out in it because of a lack of statistical power in subgroup analyses (p. 3).

Billioti de Gage et al., prospective population-based study (BMJ 2012;345:e6231): about 50% increased risk within 15 years of starting benzodiazepines, delayed in time and so, in the authors' view, not reverse causation (as described on p. 3).

Gray et al., prospective cohort with research-standard dementia diagnosis: raised hazard only at low cumulative use and none at the highest; its interval for the top category excludes the 1.84 reported here, and it attributes the difference largely to claims-based diagnosis.

replication.where_it_stands: Contested. This study and the 2012 prospective population-based study by the same first author report associations; Gray et al. (2016), with research diagnoses, covariates collected from participants and lags of 1 to 5 years, found none with the heaviest use. A meta-analysis on the project's benzodiazepine list that adjusts for protopathic bias (Penninkilampi and Eslick, 2018) was not read for this card.
